titre: December 25: Christmas, Sol Invictus, and the Chronography of 354
accroche: The oldest document that dates the birth of Christ to December 25 itself dates from the year 354.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Christmas was placed on December 25 to replace the pagan festival of the Unconquered Sun.” The line can be read everywhere, with the confidence of an established fact. The document that serves as the starting point for the whole debate comes down to a single line of Latin.

## One Line in a Calendar

In 354, in Rome, the calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus produced, for a wealthy Christian named Valentinus, an illustrated collection of chronological texts, known today as the Chronography of 354. In it, in the list of the burials of martyrs, on the very first line, is the entry: *VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae*, that is, “the eighth day before the Kalends of January, birth of Christ in Bethlehem of Judea.” The eighth day before the Kalends of January is December 25. It is the oldest known document that places the birth of Jesus on December 25.

The same collection carries, on the same date, a mention of Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun. Historians of the liturgy date the list of burials to about 336, a few years before the collection itself; the festival of the Sun is attached to the emperor Aurelian, in 274.

## Two Hypotheses, and No Verdict

The proximity of the two festivals on the same page fuels the replacement thesis: the Church supposedly chose the date of a solar cult to make people forget it. But the document indicates neither which festival came first nor whether one answers the other. It only shows that, around the middle of the 4th century, they coexisted in Rome.

Another explanation has been put forward: the calculation hypothesis, formulated by the historian Louis Duchesne. March 25, the date the Romans gave to the spring equinox, would be that of the Annunciation, hence of the conception of Christ; nine months later, you land on December 25. Duchesne himself acknowledged that this belief in a conception on March 25 is found in no early Christian text. It does not need the solar cult.

## What This Changes

The usual sentence presents as a certainty what the evidence does not settle: we have a date, attested in 354, and two competing accounts of origin, neither demonstrated by the document itself. Nor is the Christian festival a late invention: it appears in a Roman Christian calendar of the 4th century.

The document most cited in the debate does not say which of the two copied the other.

repere.texte: Chronography of 354, first entry of the Depositio martyrum: “VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae,” that is, December 25; the oldest document that places the birth of Christ on this date.
repere.source: The Chronography of 354 AD, Part 12: Commemorations of the Martyrs (MGH Chronica Minora I, 1892, pp. 71–72), tertullian.org

carte.punch: In 354, a Roman calendar notes the birth of Christ on December 25, in a single line.
carte.idee: The Chronography of 354 places the birth of Christ on December 25 and mentions the Unconquered Sun on the same date. The document does not establish which of the two festivals came first: the replacement hypothesis and the calculation from the Annunciation remain competing.

quiz.question: What does the Chronography of 354 demonstrate about the date of Christmas?
choix: That Christmas was chosen to erase the cult of the Unconquered Sun
That the date is attested in Rome in 354, without saying which festival came first
That December 25 was calculated from the Annunciation
That Christmas already existed in this form in the 2nd century, in Rome
quiz.explication: The document attests the date and the coexistence of the two festivals. It says nothing about their order or their link, and does not go back to the 2nd century.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the so-called calculation hypothesis put forward to explain December 25?
choix: A conception of Christ on March 25, nine months before the birth
A decree of the emperor Aurelian in 274
The solstice measured by the astronomers of Alexandria
A shift of the Jewish Festival of Lights
quiz_supplementaire.explication: March 25, the Roman date of the spring equinox, would be that of the Annunciation; nine months later you arrive at December 25. It does not appeal to the solar cult.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who produced the Chronography of 354, and for whom?
choix: Filocalus, for a Roman Christian named Valentinus
Eusebius of Caesarea, for Pope Julius I
Jerome, for the community of Bethlehem
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus composed it for Valentinus. The other three names have no connection with this collection.
